label: Register-transfer level design
lesson:
# Register-transfer level design

Register-transfer level (RTL) is the abstraction at which almost all digital hardware is written and at which the EDA flow begins. An RTL description says which values are stored in registers and how each register's next value is computed from the current state and inputs, once per clock cycle. Everything downstream (synthesis, equivalence checking, timing, placement) consumes or preserves this contract, so a tool designer must know exactly what RTL fixes and what it leaves open.

## Registers and next-state logic

An RTL design is a synchronous state machine written at word level. The state is the set of registers $s$; the inputs are $x$; on every active clock edge each register takes the value of a next-state function, $s_{n+1} = f(s_n, x_n)$, and outputs are $y_n = g(s_n, x_n)$. The functions $f$ and $g$ are combinational: words of bits combined by operators such as +, comparisons, multiplexers and bitwise logic.

The transfer acc ← acc + x describes two components: a register holding acc and an adder computing acc + x from its output. A synthesizer builds exactly that, a register and the adder that feeds it. Three registers with no inputs and a reset therefore evolve deterministically: their values after ten cycles are $f$ applied ten times to the reset state. Nothing about gates, delays or placement appears in the description.

## The cycle-accurate abstraction

RTL ignores propagation delay inside the combinational logic. That is legitimate only because of synchronous design: timing closure guarantees that every path settles before the next capturing edge, so only the settled values at the edges matter. This is also why RTL simulation is fast. A 32-bit addition is one operation per cycle at RTL, but dozens of gate evaluations, each a potential event, in a gate-level simulation.

The abstraction also explains what two designs have in common. A ripple-carry adder and a prefix adder that produce the same sum are the same RTL; they differ in delay and area, which RTL semantics cannot see. Writing a * b fixes the function and the cycle in which the product appears, and leaves the architecture (array, Booth, Wallace tree) to synthesis, which picks it from constraints.

## What later tools may change

Synthesis must preserve the observable behavior: the sequence of outputs for every input sequence from reset. It need not preserve internal registers. Re-encoding a state machine from binary to one-hot, or retiming registers across logic, changes which values are stored where but not what leaves the block. This has a direct consequence for verification. When registers correspond one to one, equivalence reduces to comparing the combinational logic between matched registers; after re-encoding or retiming, correspondence is lost and a sequential method is required.

RTL is also the handoff point between front end and back end. High-level synthesis outputs RTL because the whole implementation flow consumes it. The cost of an RTL bug grows with the stage at which it is found: a functional fix after layout reruns synthesis, placement, routing and timing, unless an engineering change order (ECO) can patch the netlist locally.

## Going deeper

Harris and Harris, "Digital Design and Computer Architecture", chapters 3 and 4; Micheli, "Synthesis and Optimization of Digital Circuits", chapter 1.

problems.q:
In the RTL statement 'on every rising edge, acc becomes acc + x', what does a synthesizer build?

A) A register for acc whose input is an adder fed by acc and x

B) A latch that is transparent while the clock is high

C) An adder with no storage, because + is combinational

D) A counter that ignores x
problems.a: A register for acc whose input is an adder fed by acc and x
problems.e: The transfer acc <- acc + x maps to a register (the storage) and the combinational adder that computes its next state.

problems.q:
Which piece of information is fixed by an RTL description and not left to synthesis?

A) The exact gate-level structure of the adders

B) Which standard cells implement each operator

C) The physical location of each register

D) Which values are stored in registers on each clock cycle
problems.a: Which values are stored in registers on each clock cycle
problems.e: RTL is cycle-accurate at register boundaries. The implementation of the combinational clouds is synthesis's job.

problems.q:
In the RTL statement 'on every rising edge, acc becomes acc + x', what does a synthesizer build?

A) A register for acc whose input is an adder fed by acc and x

B) A latch that is transparent while the clock is high

C) An adder with no storage, because + is combinational

D) A counter that ignores x
problems.a: A register for acc whose input is an adder fed by acc and x
problems.e: The transfer acc <- acc + x maps to a register (the storage) and the combinational adder that computes its next state.

problems.q:
Why does an RTL model simulate much faster than a gate-level netlist of the same design?

A) It ignores all inputs

B) It skips the registers entirely

C) It evaluates word-level operations once per cycle instead of propagating events through thousands of gates

D) It uses a faster clock frequency
problems.a: It evaluates word-level operations once per cycle instead of propagating events through thousands of gates
problems.e: One 32-bit add is one operation at RTL but dozens of gate evaluations, each potentially scheduling events, at gate level.

problems.q:
Two RTL designs produce identical register values on every cycle for every input sequence, but one uses a ripple-carry adder and the other a prefix adder. At the RTL abstraction they are

A) Equivalent: RTL semantics do not see gate structure or delay

B) Different, because their delays differ

C) Equivalent only if they also have the same area

D) Different, because they have different gate counts
problems.a: Equivalent: RTL semantics do not see gate structure or delay
problems.e: RTL describes behavior per cycle. Adder architecture is an implementation choice that timing and area, not RTL semantics, distinguish.

problems.q:
A designer writes an RTL multiplier as a single * operator. What does that leave open?

A) The multiplier architecture, which synthesis chooses from area and timing constraints

B) The bit width of the result, which synthesis guesses

C) The cycle in which the product is available

D) Whether the product is computed at all
problems.a: The multiplier architecture, which synthesis chooses from area and timing constraints
problems.e: Writing * fixes the function and the cycle; the architecture (array, Booth, Wallace tree) is left to the synthesizer.

problems.q:
Synthesis re-encodes a state machine from binary to one-hot. Why is that allowed even though RTL is 'cycle-accurate'?

A) Only the observable behavior at the outputs must be preserved, and the internal state encoding is not observable

B) Because RTL does not define registers

C) It is never allowed

D) Because one-hot uses fewer flip-flops
problems.a: Only the observable behavior at the outputs must be preserved, and the internal state encoding is not observable
problems.e: FSM extraction and re-encoding change internal registers but keep the input-output sequence, so equivalence must be checked sequentially, not register by register.

problems.q:
Retiming moves registers across combinational logic. What does that do to an RTL-to-netlist equivalence check?

A) Nothing: the check is unaffected

B) Register correspondence is lost, so a purely combinational check no longer applies and a sequential method is needed

C) It makes the check trivial

D) It removes all registers
problems.a: Register correspondence is lost, so a purely combinational check no longer applies and a sequential method is needed
problems.e: Combinational equivalence pairs up registers. After retiming the registers hold different values, so the tool must reason over sequences.

problems.q:
Why do high-level synthesis tools output RTL rather than gates?

A) RTL is faster silicon than gates

B) RTL is the stable handoff that existing logic synthesis, verification and timing flows consume

C) Gates cannot be generated by software

D) Logic synthesis requires C++ input
problems.a: RTL is the stable handoff that existing logic synthesis, verification and timing flows consume
problems.e: HLS fixes the schedule and the registers, then hands the resulting RTL to the standard flow.

label: Behavioral versus structural modeling
lesson:
# Behavioral versus structural modeling

Hardware description languages let a designer say what a circuit does (behavioral style) or what it is made of (structural style), with continuous-assignment dataflow in between. The distinction matters to tool builders because each style asks a different amount of work from the compiler: structural code is already a netlist, while behavioral code must be inferred into one. Real designs mix the styles, and synthesizer outputs are always structural.

## Structural descriptions are netlists

A structural description instantiates components and wires their ports together. In Verilog, and g1 (y, a, b); or g2 (z, y, c); is structural: two gate primitives and three nets, with no statement of behavior other than what the components themselves do. Module instances work the same way at any level, from a full adder to a processor core.

The natural data structure is a hypergraph. Instances are nodes and nets are hyperedges connecting every pin they touch; a net driving four loads is one hyperedge of five pins. A synthesized gate-level netlist written as Verilog is exactly this: instances of library cells joined by wires, with nothing procedural. Because the function is implied entirely by the components and their connections, a structural netlist needs no inference: a tool reads it and has the graph.

## Behavioral and dataflow descriptions

A behavioral description states function without choosing components. An always block with if statements, case statements and loops is behavioral; so is any testbench, which uses delays, file I/O and other constructs that only simulation supports. Between the two sits dataflow: assign y = (a & b) | c; describes a combinational equation that continuously drives a net, naming no gates and having no procedural sequencing.

For synthesis, behavioral code must be turned into components. A for loop over the bits of a vector, with a constant bound, is unrolled into replicated logic. A clocked always block becomes registers plus their next-state logic. The payoff is productivity: the designer writes what is computed, and a change of function is a change of a few statements rather than of a netlist.

## What each style costs a tool

Inference is the price of behavioral code. The synthesizer applies rules (a clocked block yields flip-flops, an incompletely assigned combinational block yields latches, an array with a matching access pattern yields a RAM) to deduce components. Structural code skips this step, which is why designers hand-instantiate cells whose exact form matters, such as clock-gating cells, synchronizers or pads, inside otherwise behavioral RTL.

Simulation cost runs the other way. A gate-level netlist simulates far slower than its RTL, because each gate is a separate process with its own events instead of one word-level operation. Equivalence checking connects the two worlds: to compare behavioral RTL with its synthesized netlist, the checker first reduces the RTL to a logic graph (often an and-inverter graph) using simple, trusted rules, then compares functions at matched registers with SAT or BDD methods.

## Going deeper

Thomas and Moorby, "The Verilog Hardware Description Language", chapters on structural and behavioral modeling; the Yosys manual, chapter on the Verilog front end.

problems.e: Structural code only instantiates and connects components. The others describe behavior that a tool must turn into components.

B) An initial block

problems.a: The tool must deduce registers, latches and logic from statements, whereas structural code names them directly
problems.e: Inference rules (clocked block means flop, incomplete assignment means latch) turn behavior into components; structural code already lists them.

A) RTL simulation ignores the clock

B) Gate-level netlists have more inputs

C) Every gate is a separate process with its own events instead of one word-level operation

D) Gate-level simulation uses a different language
problems.a: Every gate is a separate process with its own events instead of one word-level operation
problems.e: Structural detail multiplies the number of evaluations and events by roughly the gate count per operator.

problems.q:
A team hand-instantiates a specific clock-gating cell in otherwise behavioral RTL. Why?

A) To make simulation slower

B) To pin down a component whose exact structure matters and should not be left to inference

C) Because clock gating cannot be described any other way in simulation

D) Because behavioral code cannot express AND
problems.a: To pin down a component whose exact structure matters and should not be left to inference
problems.e: Mixed style is common: structural instances for cells that must be exact, behavioral code for everything else.

label: Four-state logic values
lesson:
# Four-state logic values

Verilog and SystemVerilog simulate with four values per bit: 0, 1, x (unknown) and z (high impedance). The extra two values let a simulator represent uninitialized registers, conflicting drivers and undriven nets, and they propagate through logic by precise rules. A tool builder must know those rules exactly, because a simulator, a linter and an equivalence checker that disagree about x produce contradictory verdicts on the same design.

## Bitwise operators on x and z

At the input of a logic operator, z behaves exactly like x: an undriven value is unknown to the gate reading it. The rules then follow from asking whether the unknown input could change the output. For AND, a 0 on either input forces 0, so $0 \wedge x = 0$, while $1 \wedge x = x$. For OR, a 1 forces 1, so $1 \vee x = 1$ and $0 \vee x = x$.

Work lane by lane on vectors. With a = 4'b10xz and b = 4'b1101, a & b is 4'b100x: lane 3 is 1 & 1 = 1, lane 2 is 0 & 1 = 0, lane 1 is x & 0 = 0, and lane 0 is z & 1 = x. Three classic mistakes give different answers: letting z pass through unchanged, reading unknowns as 0, and making every lane with an unknown input x even when the other input controls it.

## XOR, XNOR and inversion

XOR has no controlling value: flipping either input always flips the output. So any x or z input makes the XOR lane x, and the same holds for XNOR (written ~^ or ^~). Inversion maps 0 to 1 and 1 to 0, and maps both x and z to x.

Compound expressions are evaluated operator by operator. For a & ~b with a = 4'b1x01 and b = 4'b0z11, first ~b = 4'b1x00, then AND with a gives 4'b1x00: lane 2 is x & x = x, and lanes 1 and 0 are forced to 0 by the zeros of ~b. The structure of the rules mirrors the Boolean algebra of cofactors: an unknown input matters exactly when the output differs between its two possible values.

## Reductions and the two equalities

Reduction operators fold a vector to one bit with the same rules: &a is 0 if any bit is 0, otherwise x if any bit is unknown, otherwise 1. |a is 1 if any bit is 1, otherwise x or 0. ^a is x as soon as any bit is unknown.

Equality comes in two forms with different purposes. Logical equality a == b returns 0 if some lane holds two known, different bits; otherwise it returns x if any lane holds x or z; otherwise 1. Case equality a === b compares the four-state values literally, so x matches only x and z only z, and the result is always 0 or 1. That makes === useful in testbenches (checking that a signal really is x) and meaningless in hardware, where no gate can detect x. Synthesis therefore reduces === to == or rejects it, and a tool must never let x-semantics leak into a netlist.

## Going deeper

IEEE Std 1800-2017, clause 11.4 (operators) and table 11-6; Sutherland, "I'm Still in Love with My X!" (DVCon 2013).

label: Modules, ports and design hierarchy
prereqs: Pre-order and post-order traversal of a rooted tree
lesson:
# Modules, ports and design hierarchy

A module is the unit of definition in Verilog and SystemVerilog, and instances of modules form the design hierarchy. Elaboration builds that hierarchy, synthesis may keep or flatten it, and every report names objects by their hierarchical path. Tool builders need a precise picture of how ports bind, what graph the hierarchy forms and what a tool may do with module boundaries.

## Ports and connections

A module declares ports with directions: input, output or inout (bidirectional, typically tristate pads). An instance binds expressions to those ports in one of two ways. Named binding, adder u1 (.y(s), .a(x), .b(z)), connects by port name, so order does not matter. Positional binding, adder u2 (s, x, z), connects the first expression to the first declared port, and so on; if the declaration is (input a, input b, output y), s drives a, which is almost certainly a bug.

A module is a definition; an instance is one use of it, with its own state and its own connections. Width mismatches between a port and the signal connected to it are legal in Verilog and follow assignment rules (truncation or extension), which is why lint tools flag them: they rarely mean what the designer intended.

## The instance tree

Instances form a rooted tree: each instance has exactly one parent and the top module is the root. Module definitions form a directed acyclic graph instead, because one definition may be used under several parents. A register is named by its hierarchical path, such as top.cpu.alu.acc, and two instances of the same module have distinct registers with distinct paths: hardware is never shared between instances.

Counting is a tree computation. If top has 3 instances of core and each core has 2 instances of lane, there are $3 \times 2 = 6$ lanes. The definition graph must be acyclic, because a module that instantiates itself describes infinite hardware. Recursion is legal only when a parameter-dependent generate condition stops it during elaboration.

## What tools do with boundaries

A tool may keep hierarchy or flatten it. Keeping it allows separate compilation, per-block reuse and smaller problems for each run, at the cost of optimization across boundaries: a constant tied to a submodule's input cannot propagate inside while the boundary remains. Flattening removes the boundaries and exposes that optimization.

Two further mechanisms come from boundaries. A black box is a module known only by its ports, used for IP and macros implemented elsewhere; the tool connects to it but cannot see inside. Uniquification is needed when instances of one module diverge, for example because their inputs are tied to different constants and optimization treats them differently: each divergent instance needs its own definition before it can be optimized on its own.

## Going deeper

IEEE Std 1800-2017, clause 23 (modules and hierarchy); the Yosys manual entries for hierarchy, flatten and uniquify.

label: The Verilog event scheduler
lesson:
# The Verilog event scheduler

Verilog simulation semantics are defined by an event scheduler: processes wake on events, run, and schedule further events into ordered regions of each time step. Nonblocking assignment, races, testbench timing and the behavior of every compiled simulator follow from this model. A tool designer who builds a simulator, a linter or a compiled model must reproduce it or deliberately pick one of the orders it allows.

## Regions of a time step

Each simulation time step is processed in ordered regions. The active region holds ordinary work: blocking assignments, updates of continuous assignments, evaluation of the right-hand sides of nonblocking assignments and resumption of processes. The inactive region holds events delayed by #0. The NBA region holds the left-hand-side updates of nonblocking assignments. Finally, the monitor region (postponed in SystemVerilog, which adds more regions such as observed and reactive) runs monitor and strobe output.

The simulator empties the active region, moves inactive events in, and only when both are empty does it apply the NBA updates, which may wake more processes and refill the active region. This ordering is why a flip-flop modeled with <= samples old values: every right-hand side is read in the active region before any NBA update lands. It also explains why strobe shows settled values while display, which executes immediately, may show intermediate ones.

## Processes and sensitivity

Every always block, continuous assignment and gate is a process that waits for events. A continuous assignment assign y = a & b; re-evaluates when a or b changes value. An always block resumes when its event control fires. When no events remain at the current time, the simulator advances time to the earliest scheduled future event rather than stepping through empty time units, which makes event-driven simulation efficient when activity is sparse: only the fan-out of a change is evaluated.

An incomplete sensitivity list breaks the model. With always @(a) y = a & b;, a change on b alone does not wake the block, so y keeps its old value. Synthesis ignores sensitivity lists and builds an AND gate, so simulation and hardware disagree. Writing always @(*) or always_comb makes the simulator derive the list from the code and removes this class of mismatch.

## Races

Processes triggered by the same event execute in an order the standard leaves unspecified. Two clocked blocks, one doing a = b; and the other b = a; with blocking assignments, may end with both holding a's old value or both holding b's: the result is a race, and different simulators may legitimately differ. The standard fix is a coding rule: use nonblocking assignments for every variable written in a clocked block and read by another, so every process reads pre-edge values and order no longer matters.

Testbenches race too. If a testbench drives an input with a blocking assignment at the same posedge where the design samples it, one simulator may capture the new value and another the old. Driving on the opposite edge, using nonblocking assignments or using SystemVerilog clocking blocks fixes it. Compiled simulators such as Verilator choose one static order, which is just one of the legal ones, so racy code is a portability bug, not a simulator bug.

label: Blocking and nonblocking assignments
lesson:
# Blocking and nonblocking assignments

Verilog has two procedural assignments. Blocking assignment (=) updates its variable immediately; nonblocking assignment (<=) samples its right-hand side now and updates after the block has run. The difference decides whether a clocked block describes a shift register or a single register, and it is the most common source of RTL bugs. Every simulator and synthesizer must implement the two exactly, so this concept is computed, not memorized.

## Nonblocking: sample now, update later

A nonblocking assignment evaluates its right-hand side in the active region and schedules the update for the NBA region. Within one clock edge, every statement therefore reads the values from before the edge. Take a = 1, b = 2, c = 3 and the block

always @(posedge clk) begin a <= b; b <= c; c <= a; end

After one edge, a = 2, b = 3 and c = 1: the three values rotate, regardless of statement order. After a second edge they rotate again to a = 3, b = 1, c = 2. This is exactly what three flip-flops wired in a ring do, which is why nonblocking assignment is the rule for clocked logic.

## Blocking: update immediately

A blocking assignment updates its variable before the next statement runs, so later statements see the new value. With the same starting values, the block a = b; b = c; c = a; gives a = 2, b = 3 and then c = a = 2: the first value is lost. Order now matters. Reversing the statements to c = a; b = c; a = b; gives c = 1, b = 1, a = 1.

Inside combinational blocks this immediacy is what you want: blocking assignments describe a sequence of intermediate values, exactly like variables in software, and synthesis builds the corresponding chain of logic. Compilers make this precise with static single assignment: each blocking write creates a new version of the variable, and each read refers to the most recent version above it.

## Mixing the two in one block

In a mixed block, execute statements in order, apply blocking updates immediately and collect nonblocking updates until the end. With a = 2, b = 9, c = 8 and the block b <= c + 2; a = c + a; c = a + 4;, the first statement schedules b = 10; the second sets a = 10; the third reads the new a and sets c = 14. After the edge b becomes 10.

Mixing is legal but dangerous. A blocking write to a variable that another clocked block reads reintroduces races, and lint tools warn about blocking and nonblocking writes to the same variable. A common safe idiom does use both: blocking writes to a local temporary that is written before it is read, followed by nonblocking writes of the registers, which models intermediate logic feeding flip-flops.

## Going deeper

Cummings, "Nonblocking Assignments in Verilog Synthesis, Coding Styles That Kill!" (SNUG 2000); IEEE Std 1800-2017, clauses 10.4.1 and 10.4.2.

lesson:
# Flip-flop inference from clocked blocks

Synthesis does not see flip-flops in RTL; it infers them. The rule is about lifetimes: a variable needs storage when its value must survive from one clock cycle to the next. Counting inferred flip-flop bits is a direct test of whether you read a clocked block the way a synthesizer does, and getting it wrong is how designs gain phantom registers or lose intended ones.

## Every nonblocking target is a register

In always @(posedge clk), each variable assigned with <= becomes a flip-flop as wide as the variable. A conditional assignment such as if (en) q <= d; is still a register; on cycles where en is low it keeps its value, so synthesis builds a flip-flop with an enable (or a feedback multiplexer). A reset branch adds a reset or set to the same flip-flop; it does not add a second one. Continuous assignments, by contrast, never infer storage.

Count bits, not variables. With reg [7:0] q1 and reg [11:0] q2 both assigned with <= in a clocked block, and a 4-bit continuous assign elsewhere, synthesis infers $8 + 12 = 20$ flip-flop bits before optimization. Later passes may remove some (a register with a constant input, or one whose output is unused), which is why the count is stated before optimization.

## Blocking temporaries written before read

A clocked block may also contain blocking assignments to temporaries: t = a + b; q <= t;. Here t is written before it is read on every execution of the block, so no read ever sees a value from a previous cycle. Its value lives only within the edge, and synthesis turns t into a wire carrying the sum. No flip-flop is built for t, provided nothing outside the block reads it.

The test is the same one a compiler applies with liveness: is the variable live on entry to the block? A written-before-read temporary is dead on entry, because every path overwrites it first. Adding the temporary changes the flop count by zero. In the example q1 (1 bit), q2 (4), q3 (16) and an 8-bit temporary written before read, the count is $1 + 4 + 16 = 21$.

## Temporaries read before written

Reverse the order and the meaning changes: q1 <= t1; t1 = b - a;. Now the read of t1 sees the value written on the previous clock edge, so t1 must be stored across cycles. Synthesis infers a flip-flop for t1, and q1 receives a twice-delayed difference: the hardware is a two-stage pipeline although only one nonblocking assignment appears.

This is a classic accidental register. The rule generalizes: a variable assigned in a clocked block needs storage if some read of it, inside or outside the block, can observe a value from an earlier cycle. Reads before writes, reads on paths where the write is skipped, and reads from other blocks all count. Lint tools warn about blocking assignments in clocked blocks for this reason, and a counting exercise such as q1 (3 bits), q2 (4), a 16-bit temporary read before written and a 16-bit temporary written before read gives $3 + 4 + 16 = 23$.

## Going deeper

label: Inferred latches
lesson:
# Inferred latches

A combinational always block that does not assign a variable on every path forces synthesis to remember the old value on the missing paths, and the only hardware that remembers without a clock is a latch. Inferred latches are among the most common RTL defects: they complicate timing analysis, break scan insertion and often reflect a forgotten else. Counting them precisely is what a lint or synthesis tool does.

## Incomplete if statements

In always @(*), a variable must receive a value on every path through the block. if (s) y = a; with no else leaves y unassigned when s is 0, so its value must hold: synthesis builds a level-sensitive latch enabled by s. Each such variable contributes its full width in latch bits.

The cheapest cure is a default assignment at the top of the block, such as y = 0;, placed before the if. Then every path assigns y, the last assignment wins, and synthesis builds a multiplexer. For example, with y1 (8 bits) and y2 (4 bits) assigned only inside if (s) and y3 (2 bits) defaulted at the top, the block infers $8 + 4 = 12$ latch bits.

## If/else with uneven assignments

An if with an else covers both values of the condition, but only if each variable is assigned in both arms. With if (s) begin y1 = a; y3 = b; end else begin y3 = a; end, y3 is complete and becomes a multiplexer, while y1 is assigned only when s is 1 and becomes a latch. The rule per variable is: no latch if the variable has a default, or if it is assigned in every arm.

This is a reaching-definitions question in disguise. At the end of the block, ask whether every path delivers a definition of the variable. If some path delivers only the value from before the block, that value must be stored. Compilers use the same analysis, and the Yosys pass that creates the latch, proc_dlatch, runs exactly at this point.

## Case statements and full coverage

A case statement is complete for a variable only if the variable is assigned in every item and the items cover every selector value. With a 2-bit selector, four items 2'd0 to 2'd3 cover all values, so a variable assigned in all four needs no latch. With only three items, the fourth value leaves every variable unassigned, so each one latches unless a default item assigns it or a default assignment precedes the case.

Two traps deserve names. First, synthesis pragmas such as full_case tell synthesis to treat missing values as don't-cares and avoid the latch, but simulation still holds the old value, which creates a simulation-synthesis mismatch. Second, a default item assigns only the variables written in it; a variable missing from the default still latches. SystemVerilog's always_comb asks tools to report any such latch.

## Going deeper

The Yosys manual, the proc_dlatch pass; Mills and Cummings, "RTL Coding Styles That Yield Simulation and Synthesis Mismatches" (SNUG 1999).

label: case, casez and casex matching
lesson:
# case, casez and casex matching

Verilog has three case statements that differ only in how they treat x and z bits: case, casez and casex. The differences decide which item executes when a selector carries unknown bits, so they determine whether simulation hides a bug or exposes it. Synthesis reads all three as multiplexers, so a tool designer must know exactly where simulation and hardware diverge.

## casez and wildcard items

All three forms try the items in order and execute the first one that matches; later matches are ignored, which makes a case statement a priority structure unless the items are mutually exclusive. In casez, a z bit, which may be written as ?, is a wildcard: it matches anything in that position.

Take sel = 4'b1100 and the items 4'b??0? (y = 1), 4'b1?0? (y = 2), 4'b001? (y = 3). The first item checks only bit 1, which is 0, so it matches and y = 1 even though the second item also matches. Casez with ? is the standard way to write priority decoders and instruction decoders with don't-care fields.

## Unknown bits in the selector

casez also treats z in the selector as a wildcard. If sel = 4'b000z, an item 4'b0000 matches, because the z lane matches anything. That is surprising, since the selector really is unknown in that lane. Plain case is stricter: it compares like ===, so every bit including x and z must match literally. In plain case, ? is simply another spelling of z and matches only a z on the selector.

The consequence is that a selector driven by an undriven or floating net may silently match a casez item in simulation, while plain case falls through to the default. Choosing case for decoders whose selector should never be unknown keeps that failure visible.

## casex and x-masking

casex extends the wildcard to x as well as z, in both the item and the selector. With sel = 4'b100x, the item 4'b1xx0 matches because its middle lanes are wildcards and the selector's last lane is x, which also matches anything. Worse, a selector that is entirely x, such as an uninitialized register, matches the first item, so simulation proceeds as if a valid value were present.

This is x-optimism: the simulator chooses a definite branch where real hardware might do anything. Coding guidelines therefore discourage casex in RTL and prefer casez with explicit ? wildcards, or SystemVerilog's case inside, which treats only the item's x and z (and ?) as wildcards and never the selector's. For synthesis all forms become the same multiplexer logic, so the choice affects only how honestly simulation reports unknowns.

## Going deeper

IEEE Std 1800-2017, clauses 12.5.1 and 12.5.4; Mills, "Yet Another Latch and Gotchas Paper" and Sutherland, "Gotcha Again" (SNUG).

label: The synthesizable subset
lesson:
# The synthesizable subset

Verilog was designed for simulation, and only part of it describes hardware. The synthesizable subset is the part that logic synthesis maps to gates, registers and memories; the rest serves testbenches. A tool builder must know where the boundary lies, what synthesis silently ignores, and which constructs synthesize but behave differently in simulation, because those mismatches are where real bugs hide.

## Constructs synthesis ignores or rejects

Delays such as assign #5 y = a & b; are ignored by synthesis, with a warning: hardware timing comes from cells and wires, not from annotations. Printing system tasks and file I/O are skipped. General event waits inside procedural code, fork and join, and forever loops that toggle clocks describe testbench sequencing and are rejected.

Initial blocks depend on the target. FPGA configuration can load initial register values, so FPGA synthesis honors simple initial assignments; ASIC flip-flops power up unknown, so ASIC flows ignore them and state must come from reset logic. Writing RTL that relies on initial values therefore works on an FPGA and fails on an ASIC, a portability trap worth knowing when building flows for both.

## Static loops, functions and memories

A loop is synthesizable when its trip count is known at compile time. for (i = 0; i < 8; i = i + 1) y[i] = a[7 - i]; unrolls into eight wire connections, and the 32-bit integer loop variable disappears entirely, because each unrolled copy sees a constant. A loop bounded by an input port describes no fixed hardware and is rejected.

Functions without timing controls are inlined as combinational logic at each call. Arrays such as reg [7:0] mem [0:255] are recognized by memory inference: if the read and write pattern matches a RAM the target provides, synthesis maps the array to a block RAM or macro; otherwise it falls back to flip-flops and multiplexers, which for large arrays is enormous. Writing memories in the pattern a tool recognizes is a real design skill.

## Simulation-synthesis mismatches

The dangerous constructs are those that synthesize but mean something else in simulation. An incomplete sensitivity list makes simulation miss changes that the synthesized gate responds to. A full_case pragma tells synthesis that unlisted case values are don't-cares while simulation holds the outputs. Assigning y = 1'bx in an unused branch lets synthesis choose any value that minimizes logic while simulation shows x. The === operator compares x literally, which no hardware can do.

The defensive style follows directly: use always @(*) or always_comb, give every combinational output a default at the top of the block, prefer SystemVerilog unique and priority over pragmas, and verify the netlist against the RTL with an equivalence checker. Each rule removes one gap between the two models a tool chain maintains.

## Going deeper

IEEE Std 1364.1-2002 (Verilog register-transfer level synthesis); Mills and Cummings, "RTL Coding Styles That Yield Simulation and Synthesis Mismatches" (SNUG 1999).

lesson:
# Expression bit widths under Verilog sizing rules

Every Verilog expression has a bit width determined by fixed rules, and many expressions are evaluated at a width set by their context rather than by their operands. These rules decide whether a carry is kept or lost and whether a comparison is done in 4 or 32 bits. A front end must implement them exactly, and a designer who misreads them writes adders that silently drop carries.

## Self-determined widths

The rules form a small table. Arithmetic and bitwise binary operators (+, -, *, /, %, &, |, ^) take the larger operand width: if a is 8 bits and b is 4, a + b is 8 bits. Comparisons and logical operators give 1 bit. A concatenation {a, b} sums its parts, and a replication {3{b}} multiplies. Unary minus and bitwise negation keep the operand width.

Apply the rules bottom up on the expression tree. With a 3 bits, c 3 bits and d 8 bits, (d | a) & (a - c) is max(max(8, 3), max(3, 3)) = 8 bits, and {d, a + c} is $8 + 3 = 11$ bits. Notice that + does not add a carry bit: the width of a + b is the larger operand width, not one more.

## Comparisons, reductions, shifts and conditionals

Four more rules complete the table. A comparison a < b or a == b returns 1 bit, although its operands are first extended to the larger of their two widths. A reduction &a, |a or ^a returns 1 bit. A shift a << n keeps the width of a; the shift amount n is self-determined and does not affect the result width. A conditional s ? x : y takes the larger of the widths of x and y; the condition s does not contribute.

So (a < b) + c has width max(1, width of c), and {2{a < b}} is 2 bits. A useful mental check: only the operands that flow into the result value can widen it. Selectors, shift amounts and conditions are evaluated on their own.

## Context-determined evaluation

Most operands are context-determined: before evaluation they are extended to the width of the whole expression, including the assignment target. In assign y = (a + b) >> 1; with a and b 8 bits and y 9 bits, the sum is computed at 9 bits, so the carry survives and the shift keeps it. With a = 176 and b = 220, a + b = 396 fits in 9 bits, and y = 198. If y were 8 bits, the sum would be computed at 8 bits, become $396 - 256 = 140$, and y would be 70.

Concatenation stops context propagation: its operands are self-determined. So assign y = {a + b} >> 1; computes the sum at 8 bits even when y is 9 bits, losing the carry. Front ends implement this as a two-pass algorithm: compute self-determined widths bottom up, then propagate the final width top down into context-determined operands.

lesson:
# Signed and unsigned expression evaluation

Whether a Verilog expression is signed decides whether its operands are sign-extended or zero-extended, and the rule is global: a single unsigned operand makes the whole expression unsigned. That rule surprises even experienced designers and produces wrong arithmetic that simulates and synthesizes consistently, so only careful reading finds it. A front end must apply it exactly, together with the sizing rules.

## Signed operands are sign-extended

Declaring a variable signed, as in logic signed [3:0] a, makes its bit pattern a two's-complement number: 4'b1110 is -2. When every operand of an expression is signed, the expression is signed, and each operand is sign-extended to the context width before the operation.

With a = 4'b1110 (-2), c = 4'b1100 (-4) and an 8-bit target, assign y = a + c; extends both to 8 bits (11111110 and 11111100) and adds them: -6, which is 250 when y is read as unsigned. The result in the low 4 bits alone would look the same either way; the difference appears only in the extended bits, which is exactly where width-mixing bugs live.

## One unsigned operand makes everything unsigned

The signedness of an expression depends only on its operands: if any operand is unsigned, the whole expression is unsigned, and all operands are zero-extended, including the ones declared signed. With a signed a = 4'b1010 and an unsigned c = 4'b1000, a + c becomes $10 + 8 = 18$ in 8 bits, not $-6 + 8 = 2$.

The signedness of the left-hand side plays no role. Declaring y signed does not make a + c signed. To get signed arithmetic with mixed operands, convert explicitly with the signed system function or a cast, so that every operand is signed before the expression is evaluated.

## Part-selects and literals

Two rules catch most remaining bugs. A part-select is always unsigned, even when it covers the whole of a signed vector: a[3:0] + c with both declared signed is unsigned, so a = 4'b1111 and c = 4'b1011 give $15 + 11 = 26$ rather than $-1 + -5$.

Literals carry signedness too. A sized based literal such as 1'b1 or 4'd3 is unsigned, so a + 1'b1 is unsigned and zero-extends a. An unsized decimal such as 1 is a signed 32-bit integer, so a + 1 is signed, and its context width is 32 bits; a = 4'b1000 (-8) gives -7, which is 249 in an 8-bit target. Writing 4'sd1 gives a signed sized literal. Linters such as Verilator flag many of these mixes, and a robust front end reports them too.

## Going deeper

IEEE Std 1800-2017, clause 11.8 (expression evaluation rules); Sutherland and Mills, "Verilog and SystemVerilog Gotchas", gotchas on signed arithmetic.

label: SystemVerilog always_ff and always_comb
lesson:
# SystemVerilog always_ff and always_comb

SystemVerilog adds always_ff, always_comb and always_latch: procedural blocks that state the designer's intent so that tools can check it. They simulate almost like the Verilog always blocks they replace, but they close several simulation-synthesis gaps and let a linter or synthesizer reject code that would not produce the intended hardware.

## Intent that tools check

always_ff declares a clocked block that must infer flip-flops; always_comb declares combinational logic; always_latch declares an intentional latch. A tool that finds a latch inferred inside always_comb must warn or error, because the code contradicts the stated intent. Without the keyword, the same latch would pass silently as a plain always block.

Each of the three also claims exclusive ownership of the variables it writes: a variable written in always_comb may not be written by any other process, including a continuous assignment. This rules out multiple-driver bugs at compile time. The keywords therefore turn coding guidelines into checked rules, which is exactly what a compiler should do with intent.

## always_comb semantics

always_comb is more than always @(*). Its implicit sensitivity list includes variables read inside functions it calls, where @(*) looks only at the block's own expressions; a change to a module-level variable read in a called function wakes always_comb but not @(*). It also runs once automatically at time zero, after initial and always blocks start, so its outputs are consistent from the beginning even if no input ever changes.

Variables written in the block are excluded from its sensitivity, so the block does not retrigger itself. A temporary written before it is read becomes a wire carrying an intermediate value, exactly as with blocking assignments in a plain combinational block. These rules make simulation match what synthesis builds.

## Clocks, types and what remains unchecked

always_ff @(posedge clk or negedge rst_n) lists two edges, and the tool must identify one as the clock and the other as an asynchronous control, from the if (!rst_n) ... else ... pattern. SystemVerilog code typically uses the four-state type logic for everything these blocks write, which removes Verilog's reg-versus-wire choice; nets with several drivers still need wire.

Some problems remain beyond the keywords. A blocking assignment inside always_ff to a variable read by another block is legal but race-prone, so linters flag it. A combinational loop through two always_comb blocks is not detected by either block's checks; it needs a loop check across the netlist. Knowing the limits of a check is part of building on it.

## Going deeper

lesson:
# The logic type, packed arrays and structs

SystemVerilog's data types give a front end most of its bookkeeping: the four-state logic type, packed arrays that form one contiguous vector, packed structs with named fields and unpacked arrays of elements. Bit counts and select widths follow from a few rules, and getting them right is the first thing elaboration and lint must do before any logic is built.

## Packed arrays

Dimensions written before the name are packed: logic [3:0][7:0] bus; is one 32-bit vector, organized as four 8-bit bytes. Packed dimensions multiply, so logic [2:0][1:0][7:0] holds $3 \times 2 \times 8 = 48$ bits. A packed array can be used anywhere a vector can: in arithmetic, in comparisons and in assignments to other vectors of the same width.

Indexing selects along the leftmost dimension first. bus[2] is the third byte, 8 bits, and bus[2][3] is one bit. The logic type is four-state and can be written by procedural blocks or by one continuous assignment; the two-state bit type models 0 and 1 only and is used where x makes no sense.

## Packed structs

A typedef struct packed groups named fields into one vector whose width is the sum of the fields. With fields logic [3:0] tag, logic valid and logic parity, the struct is $4 + 1 + 1 = 6$ bits, and the first field occupies the most significant bits. A packed array of such structs, pkt_t [3:0] q, holds $4 \times 6 = 24$ bits.

Because a packed struct is just a vector with names, it can be assigned to or from a plain vector of the same width, compared and passed through ports. Packages typically hold these typedefs, so that every module that uses a bus agrees on the field layout and total width, which is exactly the consistency an interface needs.

## Unpacked arrays and selects

Dimensions written after the name are unpacked: logic [3:0][7:0] mem [128]; is 128 separate elements, each a 32-bit packed vector. Total storage is $128 \times 4 \times 8 = 4096$ bits, but the array is not one vector: it cannot be used in arithmetic as a whole, and synthesis may map it to a memory.

Selects peel dimensions from the outside in. mem[5] is the whole packed element, 32 bits; mem[5][1] then selects along the leftmost packed dimension, an 8-bit row; mem[5][1][0] is one bit. A front end computes these widths during elaboration and type checking, and a mismatch between a select's width and its destination is one of the most common lint warnings.

## Going deeper

lesson:
# Interfaces, modports and packages

Large SystemVerilog designs repeat the same buses and the same type declarations across dozens of modules. Interfaces bundle a bus into one named port, modports give each side its directions, and packages share types and constants. A front end has to resolve all three during compilation and elaboration, and getting their ordering rules wrong is a common source of tool failures on real code.

## Interfaces bundle signals

An interface declares a group of related signals, such as the 40 wires of an AXI channel, and modules take the interface as a single port. Connecting a bus is then one connection instead of forty, and adding a signal means editing the interface once rather than every port list and every instance, which removes a whole class of drift bugs.

Interfaces can hold more than signals: tasks, functions, assertions and small procedural blocks, so a protocol checker can live next to the bus it checks. They are an elaboration-time convenience. After elaboration and flattening, an interface port has become its individual signals, connected exactly as if they had been listed one by one; synthesis sees ordinary nets.

## Modports give directions

Inside an interface every signal is just a variable or net; directions depend on who is looking. A modport defines one view: in the master view, valid and data are outputs and ready is an input; in the slave view the reverse. A module port declared with a modport gets those directions, and a write to a signal the modport lists as input is a compile-time error.

To type-check a module with an interface port, a front end needs the interface definition (signal names and widths) and the modport (directions). Interfaces often take the clock as a port so that clocking blocks and synchronous helpers inside can refer to it, keeping the bus definition self-contained.

## Packages and compile order

A package is a namespace of shared declarations: types, parameters, constants and functions. A typedef struct packed declared in a package and used for the ports of two modules guarantees that both agree on the field layout and width. Modules import from the package, either explicitly (import pkg::opcode_t;) or with a wildcard (import pkg::*;), which is resolved lazily and can make a name's origin unclear or clash with local names.

Packages are compile-time dependencies. A module that imports a package can only be analyzed after the package, so file order (or a dependency-aware compile) matters. Module instantiation is different: an instance can refer to a module defined in a later file, because elaboration links instances to definitions after all files are parsed. Build systems and front ends that ignore this distinction fail on otherwise valid code.

label: unique and priority case
lesson:
# unique and priority case

SystemVerilog's unique and priority modifiers on case and if statements state properties of the decision logic: that items never overlap, or that some item always matches. Synthesis uses the properties to build cheaper logic, and simulation checks them at run time. They replace the older full_case and parallel_case pragmas, which spoke only to synthesis and created silent mismatches.

## unique: mutually exclusive items

unique case asserts that exactly one item matches the selector, unless a default handles the remainder. Simulation reports a violation if two items match (overlap) or if none matches and there is no default. In casez with items 2'b1? and 2'b?1, the selector 2'b11 matches both, so a unique violation is reported, although the first match still executes.

The payoff in synthesis is structure. Mutually exclusive items let the tool OR the selected values together in a parallel multiplexer instead of building a priority chain, which is shallower and smaller. unique0 keeps the no-overlap check but allows no item to match. A default item satisfies the completeness check, but overlapping explicit items are still violations.

## priority: ordered but complete

priority case keeps the ordinary first-match-wins semantics, so overlap is allowed, and adds a promise that at least one item matches. A priority case with no default that sees an unmatched selector reports a violation in simulation.

Completeness is exactly what a latch would otherwise cover. Without the promise, a combinational case that leaves some selector values unassigned infers a latch; with priority, synthesis may treat the unlisted values as unreachable and build plain logic. The same keywords apply to if chains: unique if promises that the conditions are mutually exclusive, and priority if promises that some branch is taken.

## Why checked promises beat pragmas

A full_case or parallel_case pragma tells synthesis the same things, but simulation never sees it. If the promise is false, simulation holds an old value or takes the first match while the netlist does something else, and nothing reports the difference. unique and priority make both tools act on the same assumption and make simulation check it, so a broken promise appears as a violation message.

Run-time checks only cover the stimulus applied, though. A design that never violates unique in simulation can still fail in silicon on an input sequence that was never simulated. Proving the promise for all inputs needs formal tools, which can check the same properties as assertions. A common safe use is the decode of a one-hot state register, whose items are mutually exclusive by construction.

## Going deeper

# VHDL signals, variables and delta cycles

VHDL draws the line between immediate and deferred update with two kinds of object: variables, which change at once, and signals, which change only when the process suspends. Delta cycles order the resulting updates without advancing time. Verilog's blocking and nonblocking assignments are the same idea in another syntax, and every HDL simulator kernel, including SystemC's, is built on this evaluate-then-update loop.

## Signals update when the process suspends

A signal assignment a <= v + 4; inside a process schedules a new value; the signal keeps its old value until the process suspends. Every read of a signal within one activation therefore sees the value from before the activation, however many times the process assigned it. A variable assignment v := c + a; takes effect immediately, so later statements read the new value.

Take a = 3, b = 2, c = 8 and a clocked process that executes v := c + a; a <= v + 4; v := v + 4; c <= v + a; b <= b + c;. Then v = 11, a is scheduled to 15, v becomes 15, c is scheduled to $15 + 3 = 18$ (a still reads 3), and b is scheduled to $2 + 8 = 10$ (c still reads 8). After the edge, a = 15, b = 10 and c = 18.

## Variables keep their values between activations

Variables declared in a process persist from one activation to the next; they are initialized once, at elaboration. This matters when a variable is read before it is written: the read sees the value from the previous activation, and in a clocked process that variable becomes a register, exactly like a Verilog blocking temporary read before it is written.

Over several clock edges, simulate one activation at a time: run the statements with immediate variable updates and deferred signal updates, apply the signal updates, then start the next activation with the new signal values and the persisting variable values. A process that writes its variable before reading it on every path behaves as pure logic; one that does not has hidden state.

## Delta cycles

Concurrent signal assignments outside processes, such as s2 <= x or s1;, are processes sensitive to the signals they read. When input x changes in delta cycle 0, every assignment that reads x wakes and its target updates in delta 1; assignments reading those targets update in delta 2, and so on, all at the same simulation time.

A signal settles one delta after the latest of its inputs, so its final delta number is $\delta(s) = 1 + \max_{u \in \text{inputs}(s)} \delta(u)$ with $\delta(x) = 0$: the longest path from x in the dependency graph. With s1 <= not x; s2 <= x or s1; s4 <= s1 or s2;, s1 settles at delta 1, s2 at delta 2 and s4 at delta 3, whatever order the statements are written in. Delta cycles make the result independent of process order, which is the whole point of deferred update.

# VHDL std_logic and resolution functions

When several drivers drive one VHDL signal, a resolution function computes the value the signal takes. IEEE 1164's std_logic uses nine values and one resolution table to model strong and weak drivers, high impedance and unknowns. Simulators implement this table on every multiply driven net, so a tool designer must be able to apply it and to know which types allow multiple drivers at all.

## Nine values and their strengths

std_ulogic has nine values: 'U' (uninitialized), 'X' (forcing unknown), '0' and '1' (forcing values), 'Z' (high impedance), 'W' (weak unknown), 'L' and 'H' (weak 0 and weak 1) and '-' (don't care). Strength is the key idea. A forcing value comes from an active driver; a weak value comes from something like a pull-up resistor; 'Z' means not driving at all.

The resolution rule follows from strength. A forcing value beats a weak one, a weak value beats 'Z', and 'Z' with anything gives the other value. So '1' and 'Z' resolve to '1', and 'H' and 'Z' resolve to 'H'. Most std_logic signals in RTL have a single driver, and the resolution function returns that driver's value unchanged.

## Conflicts between drivers

Two different values of the same strength conflict, and the result is the unknown of that strength: '0' and '1' give 'X'; 'L' and 'H' give 'W'. A weak conflict loses to any forcing value, so 'W' and '0' give '0'. 'X' dominates every value except 'U', which dominates everything, and '-' resolves like 'X'.

With 'L' and 'H' driving the same bus the result is 'W', telling the designer that two pull resistors fight. With a pull-up 'H' and an active '0', the result is '0', which is how open-drain buses such as I2C are modeled: any device pulling low wins over the pull-up.

## Resolving many drivers

The resolution table is commutative and associative, so the result for any number of drivers is obtained by folding the table over them in any order. For drivers '0', 'H' and 'Z': '0' with 'H' gives '0', and '0' with 'Z' gives '0'. For '1', 'L' and 'X', the 'X' dominates and the result is 'X'.

Which types may have several drivers is part of the language. std_logic is resolved and allows them; std_ulogic is unresolved, so a second driver is a compile-time error, which catches accidental multiple drivers early. Synthesis maps a resolved signal with several tristate drivers to tristate buffers or, inside a chip where internal tristates are not allowed, rejects it or converts it to multiplexers.

## Going deeper

IEEE Std 1164-1993, the resolution table of std_logic; Ashenden, "The Designer's Guide to VHDL", the chapter on resolved signals.

# SystemC and transaction-level modeling

SystemC is a C++ class library with a discrete-event simulation kernel, standardized as IEEE 1666. It is used for architecture models, virtual platforms that run software before silicon exists, and as an input to high-level synthesis. For a tool designer it is a useful contrast with Verilog and VHDL: the same evaluate-update semantics, delivered as a library rather than a language.

## Modules and processes in C++

A SystemC model is an ordinary C++ program compiled with a standard compiler and linked with the SystemC kernel. SC_MODULE(adder) declares a class derived from sc_module, whose constructor creates ports, signals and processes. Processes come in two kinds. An SC_METHOD runs to completion each time an event in its sensitivity list fires; it has no stack of its own, so triggering it is a plain function call. An SC_THREAD has its own stack and can call wait() to suspend in the middle of its body, which makes sequential behavior easy to write but costs a context switch at each suspension.

A clocked SC_METHOD sensitive to clk.pos() corresponds to always @(posedge clk). Because it is all C++, models can use any library, templates and data structures, which is both SystemC's power and the reason only a subset is synthesizable.

## Evaluate-update and delta cycles

An sc_signal follows evaluate-update semantics. A process that calls s.write(5) and then s.read() sees the old value: the write is applied in the update phase, after all runnable processes have executed in the evaluate phase. One evaluate phase plus one update phase is a delta cycle, and it does not advance simulated time. Updated signals can wake more processes, so the kernel repeats delta cycles until nothing is runnable, then advances time to the next scheduled event.

This is the same mechanism as VHDL signals and Verilog nonblocking assignment, adopted for the same reason: processes that run at the same time see consistent values regardless of the order in which the kernel happens to execute them.

## Transaction-level modeling

TLM-2.0 abstracts communication away from pins. Instead of toggling address, data and handshake signals for a bus read, an initiator calls a function such as b_transport with a generic payload describing the whole transaction. A memory model answers in one call. Virtual platforms built this way run fast enough to boot an operating system.

Loosely timed models add temporal decoupling: an initiator runs ahead of simulated time and synchronizes with the kernel only once per quantum, cutting context switches at the cost of timing accuracy; approximately timed models add phases for more accurate contention. TLM models are not formally equivalent to RTL; teams connect the two through transactors, which convert transactions to cycle-level signals so that one testbench can drive either. A synthesizable SystemC subset, with bit-accurate types such as sc_uint, is a common input to high-level synthesis.

## Going deeper

# Verilog-AMS and VHDL-AMS

Verilog-AMS and VHDL-AMS extend digital HDLs with continuous-time analog behavior: voltages and currents governed by differential-algebraic equations, solved by a SPICE-like engine alongside the event-driven digital kernel. They are how analog blocks are modeled behaviorally, how compact device models are written (in the Verilog-A subset) and how mixed-signal chips are verified. Tool designers meet them in circuit simulators and mixed-signal flows.

## Disciplines and conservative quantities

Verilog-AMS describes analog signals through disciplines. The electrical discipline pairs a potential nature (voltage) with a flow nature (current). A discipline with both is conservative: when modules connect at a node, the simulator enforces Kirchhoff's laws, so currents into the node sum to zero and connected terminals share one potential. A signal-flow discipline has only a potential and models an ideal block diagram with no loading.

VHDL-AMS (IEEE 1076.1) expresses the same idea with terminals, which are analog nodes, and quantities defined across and through them: an across quantity is a voltage between terminals, a through quantity a current. Either way, the model's job is to state the branch equations; the simulator assembles the network.

## Contribution statements and the analog solver

An analog block states branch relations with the contribution operator. I(p, n) <+ V(p, n) / R; contributes a resistor's current, and I(p, n) <+ C * ddt(V(p, n)); contributes a capacitor's, where ddt is the time derivative (idt is the time integral). Contributions to the same branch add, so these two statements together model a resistor and capacitor in parallel.

The simulator combines all contributions with Kirchhoff's laws into a system of differential-algebraic equations $F(x, \dot{x}, t) = 0$ and integrates it in time, solving the nonlinear equations at each time point with Newton iteration, exactly as SPICE does for transistors. VHDL-AMS writes the equations directly as simultaneous statements, such as v == r * i;, which are declarative constraints rather than assignments.

## Mixed-signal boundaries

In a mixed-signal simulation, a digital output that drives an analog input passes through a connect module, inserted automatically according to discipline rules. It converts logic values into a voltage waveform with modeled rise and fall times; in the other direction, a comparator with a threshold turns an analog voltage into digital events, ideally with hysteresis so that noise near the threshold does not produce a storm of spurious toggles.

Every boundary crossing forces the analog solver to stop at that time point and synchronize with the digital kernel, so designs with frequent interaction simulate slowly. Compact device models written in Verilog-A are compiled for circuit simulators, for example by OpenVAF for ngspice, so that the model's currents and their derivatives are evaluated quickly inside every Newton iteration.

## Going deeper

Kundert and Zinke, "The Designer's Guide to Verilog-AMS" (2004); Accellera, the Verilog-AMS Language Reference Manual; IEEE Std 1076.1 for VHDL-AMS.

lesson:
# Lexical analysis of HDL source

Every HDL tool starts by turning characters into tokens: keywords, identifiers, numbers, operators and punctuation. The lexer is the simplest phase of a compiler, but Verilog's operator set (=== , >>>, ~&, <= used both as assignment and comparison), its preprocessor and its comments make it easy to get subtly wrong. Counting tokens by hand is the fastest way to internalize the rules a lexer implements.

## Tokens and what produces none

A token is the smallest meaningful unit of source: a keyword such as assign or posedge, an identifier such as cnt, a number such as 47, an operator such as & or <=, or punctuation such as ( ) [ ] ; and @. Whitespace and comments produce no tokens; they only separate tokens. So assign y = a & b; is seven tokens, and so is assign y=a&b;.

Before lexing proper, Verilog runs a preprocessor that expands macros, includes files and evaluates conditional compilation (ifdef). Because macros can produce arbitrary token sequences, a front end must lex the preprocessed text, and good tools keep a map from each token back to its original file and line so that error messages point at the source the user wrote.

## Maximal munch

A lexer reads greedily: at each position it takes the longest character sequence that forms a valid token. This is the maximal-munch rule. In a<=b the characters <= form one token, giving three tokens a, <=, b. In a===b the lexer takes ===, not == followed by =. Other multi-character operators include !==, <<, >>, <<<, >>>, &&, ||, **, >= and the reduction operators ~&, ~| and ~^.

The parser, not the lexer, decides what <= means. In q <= d; after an always block it is a nonblocking assignment; inside if (a <= b) it is a comparison. The lexer emits the same token in both cases, and the grammar resolves it from context. Counting tokens in if ( a <= b ) y = 1 ; gives 10, whatever the meaning.

## Comments, selects and literals

A line comment starting with // runs to the end of the line, and a block comment between /* and */ can sit anywhere between tokens; both are discarded, even when they contain text that looks like code, such as a <= b. A bit select rdy[0] is four tokens: rdy, [, 0 and ]. A plain decimal number is one token.

Sized literals such as 8'hFF are a classic lexer subtlety, because the size, the base and the digits may legally be separated by whitespace, so lexers differ in whether they treat them as one token or several; the parser then reassembles them. A lexer must also handle escaped identifiers, which begin with a backslash and end at whitespace, and keywords that depend on the language version selected, which is why tools take a language-version option before they read any file.

## Going deeper

Aho, Lam, Sethi and Ullman, "Compilers: Principles, Techniques, and Tools" (2nd ed.), chapter 3; IEEE Std 1800-2017, clause 5 (lexical conventions).

prereqs: Pre-order and post-order traversal of a rooted tree
lesson:
# Parsing and operator precedence

The parser turns the token stream into a tree according to the language grammar. For expressions the grammar encodes operator precedence and associativity, which decide what an unparenthesized expression means. Verilog has a long precedence table with several surprises, and every front end, from Icarus to slang to Yosys, must apply it identically or the same source will mean different hardware in different tools.

## Precedence levels

Precedence decides which operator binds tighter. In 4 + 2 * 3 the multiplication binds first, giving $4 + 6 = 10$, not 18. Verilog's binary operators, from tightest to loosest, are: ** ; then * / % ; then + - ; then the shifts << >> <<< >>> ; then the relational < <= > >= ; then the equalities == != === !== ; then & ; then ^ and ~^ ; then | ; then && ; then || ; and finally the conditional ?:. Unary operators bind tighter than all of them.

Fully parenthesizing an expression makes its tree explicit. 2 + 3 << 1 is (2 + 3) << 1 = 10, because + binds tighter than the shift, which surprises programmers used to other conventions.

## Bitwise operators below comparisons

The most dangerous surprise in Verilog, as in C, is that the bitwise operators bind more loosely than the comparisons. a & b == c parses as a & (b == c), a bitwise AND with a 1-bit comparison result, not as (a & b) == c. Likewise 7 & 7 == 2 * 1 is 7 & (7 == 2) = 7 & 0 = 0. And 2 < 9 << 2 == 1 parses as ((2 < (9 << 2)) == 1), which is 1.

Binary operators of equal precedence associate to the left, so 8 - 3 - 2 is (8 - 3) - 2 = 3. A precedence-climbing or Pratt parser implements all of this with one table of levels: it parses an operand, then repeatedly absorbs operators whose level is at least the current minimum, parsing each right operand at one level tighter.

## The conditional and logical operators

The conditional operator ?: has the lowest precedence and associates to the right. In 1 == 3 ? 7 & 7 : 8 | 7, the condition is (1 == 3), which is 0, so the value is the false arm (8 | 7) = 15; a ? b : c ? d : e means a ? b : (c ? d : e). The logical && binds tighter than ||, so a || b && c is a || (b && c).

Parse trees are also where front ends attach source locations, the line and column of each node, which later stages use for error messages and for the src attributes that link netlist cells back to RTL. A front end that loses them makes every downstream report harder to use.

## Going deeper

IEEE Std 1800-2017, clause 11.3.2 and table 11-2 (operator precedence); Aho, Lam, Sethi and Ullman, "Compilers", chapter 4.

lesson:
# Abstract syntax trees for HDLs

An abstract syntax tree (AST) keeps the structure of a program and drops the punctuation that only served to fix that structure. It is the first real data structure of a hardware compiler: Yosys's Verilog front end builds one, slang builds a richer one, and elaboration, type checking and lowering to netlist IRs all walk it. Counting its nodes, its height and its shared subtrees exercises what a compiler stores.

## Nodes of an expression tree

In an expression AST every operator is an internal node whose children are its operands, and every operand occurrence is a leaf. Parentheses produce no node: their only job was to choose the shape, which the tree records directly. A unary operator has one child, a binary operator two, and the conditional ?: is one node with three children.

So (t ? (2 & c) : a) ^ ~(a - d) has the operators ^, ?:, &, ~ and -, five internal nodes, and the leaf occurrences t, 2, c, a, a and d, six leaves, for 11 nodes in all. Note that a appears twice as a leaf: an AST is a tree, so a repeated operand is a repeated node. A concrete syntax tree, by contrast, would keep every token, parentheses included.

## Height and traversal

The height of a tree is the number of edges on the longest path from the root to a leaf. The root is the operator applied last, the loosest-binding one at the top level. For (1 ^ b) ^ (1 - c), the root ^ has two children of height 1, so the tree has height 2. For an expression tree the height is the depth of nesting, which for a combinational circuit built directly from it is the number of logic levels on the longest path.

Compilers walk ASTs in two orders. A post-order traversal visits children before their parent, which is how an evaluator or a code generator processes operands before the operator. A pre-order traversal visits the parent first, which is how attributes such as expected widths are pushed down, exactly the two passes Verilog's sizing rules require.

## Sharing subtrees in a DAG

Identical subtrees compute identical values, so a compiler can store each one once. Hash-consing does this: before creating a node, look up its operator and the identities of its children in a table, and reuse an existing node if one matches. The tree becomes a directed acyclic graph.

In ((2 - d) * (b ^ 1)) | (c + (2 - d)) the tree has 13 nodes. The subtree 2 - d appears twice and becomes one node, and the leaves 2 and d are shared with it, as is every repeated operand. The DAG has 10 nodes. This is common subexpression elimination performed at construction time, and it is the representation behind and-inverter graphs in ABC and the structural hashing done by every logic synthesizer. Two subtrees match only if they are written identically, operand order included, unless the compiler first puts commutative operators into a canonical order.

## Going deeper

Appel, "Modern Compiler Implementation in ML", chapter 4; Mishchenko, Chatterjee and Brayton, "DAG-Aware AIG Rewriting" (DAC 2006).

label: Elaboration
lesson:
# Elaboration

Elaboration turns a set of parsed modules into one concrete design. It picks the top, links every instance to its module, evaluates parameters and widths per instance, unrolls generate constructs and builds the instance tree. It is the phase where HDL compilers differ most and where SystemVerilog is hardest to implement, which is why shared elaborators such as slang and Surelog exist.

## What elaboration builds

Parsing checks each file against the grammar on its own. Elaboration starts from the top module and builds the design: it resolves each instance to its module definition, binds parameter values, evaluates every constant expression in declarations (so a port declared [W-1:0] gets a number), unrolls generate loops and selects generate-if branches. The result is a tree of instances in which nothing is symbolic any more.

Only what is reachable from the top is elaborated. A module that is parsed but never instantiated under the chosen top is not part of the design, although some tools treat every uninstantiated module as an extra top, which is why flows name the top explicitly. The elaborated design is what simulation and synthesis consume.

## Parameters resolve top down

A child's parameters can depend on values its parent passes in, so elaboration resolves the hierarchy top down: the parent's values are known before the child is specialized. Two instances of fifo with W = 8 and W = 16 become two specializations of fifo, one per distinct parameter set; tools name them separately (Yosys uses a paramod prefix). A generate-if on a parameter is decided per instance, so only one implementation exists for each.

defparam complicates this, because it can override a parameter from anywhere in the hierarchy, making the result depend on resolution order. Modern guidelines and tools discourage it in favor of inline #() overrides, which keep every override local to the instance it affects.

## Errors that only elaboration can see

Some errors are invisible until the design is assembled. Every file can parse cleanly while an instance names a module that no file defines. A port connection's width mismatch is only detectable once a parameter fixes the port width. Recursive instantiation terminates only if a parameter-dependent generate condition eventually fails, as when N is halved down to 1.

Because elaboration is where SystemVerilog's semantics live, building a complete elaborator is a large project. Surelog and slang each build a full elaborated model, and Surelog writes it out as UHDM so that other tools (a Yosys plug-in, Verilator, CIRCT) can consume one shared interpretation instead of implementing their own. That sharing matters because two elaborators that disagree produce two different designs from the same source.

## Going deeper

IEEE Std 1800-2017, clause 23.10 (elaboration) and clause 27 (generate constructs); the slang and Surelog documentation.

prereqs: Expression bit widths under Verilog sizing rules
lesson:
# Parameters and parameter overrides

Parameters make one module definition describe a family of hardware: a FIFO of any depth, a bus of any width. Elaboration binds a value to every parameter of every instance and evaluates every expression that depends on them, including port widths. Front ends must get the override rules exactly right, because a wrong width propagates silently into synthesis and simulation.

## Defaults and named overrides

A module declares parameters with defaults: module buffer #(parameter DEPTH = 16, parameter W = 8). A localparam such as localparam PW = W + 2*DEPTH; is derived and cannot be overridden from outside, which makes it the right place for values that must stay consistent with the others. Port widths can use both, as in output [PW-1:0] bus.

An instance overrides parameters by name: buffer #(.W(12)) u0 (...); sets W to 12 and leaves DEPTH at its default. Elaboration then evaluates the localparam for this instance, $PW = 12 + 2 \times 16 = 44$, and the bus port of u0 is 44 bits wide. Every instance is evaluated separately, so two instances with different overrides have different port widths.

## Values passed down the hierarchy

Overrides can be expressions over the parent's own parameters. If core #(parameter N = 2) instantiates buffer #(.DEPTH(N*2), .W(N+3)), and top instantiates core #(.N(6)), elaboration resolves top down: u_core gets N = 6, then u_buf gets DEPTH = 12 and W = 9, so PW = $9 + 2 \times 12 = 33$.

The order is forced: a child cannot be specialized until its parent's values are known. This is why elaboration is a top-down tree walk, and why the older defparam statement, which can override a parameter from anywhere in the hierarchy, makes the result depend on resolution order and is discouraged. Each distinct set of parameter values produces one specialized module, which later stages treat as a separate definition.

## Positional overrides

An instance can also override parameters by position: buffer #(6, 10) u0 (...); assigns the values in the order the parameters are declared in the module header. With the header #(parameter DEPTH = 4, parameter W = 8) this sets DEPTH = 6 and W = 10, giving $PW = 10 + 2 \times 6 = 22$; if the header declared W first, the same instance would set W = 6 and DEPTH = 10, giving $6 + 20 = 26$.

Positional binding therefore couples every instance to the declaration order of the module, and reordering parameters in a header silently changes every positional instance. Named overrides avoid this, which is why style guides and linters prefer them. A front end must also reject attempts to override a localparam and report overrides of parameters that do not exist, both common symptoms of a mismatch between an instance and its module.

## Going deeper
